screens.title: Custom Exceptions and Exception Propagation
screens.narratorSegment: In real applications, generic errors are not enough. You will learn why defining custom exceptions gives your code clearer contracts and richer diagnostics, and how exception propagation with the throws keyword moves responsibility up the call stack. We begin with the practical rationale: a banking withdrawal failure is more informative when represented by an InsufficientFundsException than by a generic illegal argument or runtime error. That clarity makes handling behavior explicit for callers and enables richer logging and automated responses. We'll also show the mechanical differences between checked and unchecked exceptions, when the compiler enforces handling, and when it doesn't. Finally, we'll explore exception wrapping, where lower-level causes are preserved as the underlying reason for a higher-level, domain-focused exception. As we progress, you will see code patterns for creating exceptions, declaring throws, catching and rethrowing with a cause, and trade-offs to avoid over-creating tiny exception types. By the end of this lesson, you will understand how to represent domain rules with types, propagate errors cleanly, and wrap exceptions so that the original stack and message remain available for debugging. Consider an error you recently handled: would a custom exception have made handling clearer?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will design and implement custom checked and unchecked exceptions, choose the appropriate exception type for a domain error, and use constructors to carry error details. You will understand exception propagation: how the throws keyword delegates responsibility to a caller and how an exception travels up the call stack until handled. You will practice rethrowing and wrapping exceptions so that higher-level layers see business-friendly error types while lower-level causes remain accessible through getCause. You will also learn practical restraints: avoid excessive tiny exception classes, prefer checked exceptions for recoverable, anticipated problems, and reserve unchecked exceptions for programming or unrecoverable errors. Each objective is mapped to a verified competency milestone that shows you how to test and confirm mastery: create a checked InsufficientFundsException with getters and handle it in calling code; implement a DataAccessException that wraps a SQLException and use getCause to log root failures. These skills make error handling explicit, maintainable, and easier to debug in layered applications.

screens.title: What is a Custom Exception?
screens.narratorSegment: A custom exception is simply a user-defined class that extends an existing throwable type in Java. When you extend Exception you create a checked exception: the compiler forces callers to handle or declare it. When you extend RuntimeException you create an unchecked exception: callers are not forced by the compiler to catch or declare it. The key value of a custom exception is representation. Instead of treating every failure as a generic illegal argument or null pointer, a meaningful type like InsufficientFundsException signals the exact business rule that failed and can carry structured data such as a current balance and attempted withdrawal amount. This lets handlers react differently depending on the failure type, and allows logging or automated responses that reference domain details. A common misconception is that more exception classes mean better code. In practice you should create a custom exception when its type communicates intent or enables specific handling. If the standard java exceptions already express the condition and no extra behavior or data is required, prefer the built-in types. Think of custom exceptions as part of your A P I contract: they make legal, recoverable failure modes explicit and discoverable to callers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Definition
Custom Exception — concept
A named Java class that extends Exception or RuntimeException, used to make domain errors explicit and carry additional context for handlers.
When to create one
  • When a business rule failure needs to be handled specifically by callers.
  • When you want to include structured details about the error for logging or automated responses.
  • When the standard exceptions would be ambiguous or leak implementation details.
Analogy
Like a specific error code from a device instead of a single generic "error" lamp.
Misconception
Avoid creating tiny exceptions for every minor variation; group similar failures when handling is identical.
Concrete example
// Custom checked exception
public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
  private double currentBalance;
  private double withdrawalAmount;

  public InsufficientFundsException(String message, double currentBalance, double withdrawalAmount) {
    super(message);
    this.currentBalance = currentBalance;
    this.withdrawalAmount = withdrawalAmount;
  }

  public double getCurrentBalance() { return currentBalance; }
  public double getWithdrawalAmount() { return withdrawalAmount; }
}
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use custom exceptions to express domain intent and carry structured error details that consumers can query.

Why this matters: types are documentation. When your API signals that a withdrawal can fail with InsufficientFundsException, callers can present precise messages and recover correctly.

screens.title: Checked vs Unchecked Custom Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Checked exceptions extend Exception and require callers to either catch them or declare them with throws. They are appropriate for anticipated, recoverable external conditions such as validation failures, input and output problems, or business rules the caller can reasonably address. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are not enforced by the compiler. Use them for programming errors or unrecoverable conditions where forcing callers to catch them would add noise. A common example in the chapter is InvalidAccountIdFormatException as an unchecked exception: an invalid format often indicates a programming or input validation bug that should be fixed rather than caught repeatedly. A mistake learners make is choosing unchecked for recoverable conditions, which hides the obligation to handle an expected failure. Conversely, overusing checked exceptions can force many try-catch blocks that clutter control flow. Think in terms of responsibility: if a caller can reasonably recover or present corrective UI, prefer a checked exception. If the failure signals a bug or unrecoverable state, prefer unchecked. For clarity, include constructors for message and cause, and attach domain fields when callers need them. This comparison helps you design the right contract for library and application layers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Checked vs Unchecked
Checked Exception
Extends Exception. The compiler forces handling or declaration, making recoverable errors explicit in method signatures.
When to use
  • Anticipated failures callers can reasonably recover from.
  • Business rule violations like insufficient funds or invalid product data.
Example
InsufficientFundsException extends Exception and the withdraw method declares throws.
Unchecked Exception
Extends RuntimeException. The compiler does not force handling; use for programming bugs or unrecoverable states.
When to use
  • Invalid input formats that indicate a coding or validation bug.
  • Severe initialization errors that cannot be meaningfully handled at runtime.
Example
ProductInitializationError extends RuntimeException for a rare unrecoverable setup failure.
Pro tip
Prefer checked for API-level, recoverable conditions that callers should handle explicitly.
Common mistake
Using unchecked everywhere hides obligations and can lead to runtime surprises for callers.
Check
Ask: Can the caller reasonably recover? If yes, lean checked.

screens.title: InsufficientFundsException: class and fields
screens.narratorSegment: Here we walk through a typical checked custom exception that carries domain information. The InsufficientFundsException extends Exception, includes fields for the current balance and attempted withdrawal, and provides constructors that accept a message and these values. Why include fields? Because handlers often need those numeric details to log, show a corrective message, or compute alternative flows. A common pitfall is only passing a message string; structured getters are more reliable for automated handling. Notice the implementation pattern: call super(message) to initialize the base Throwable message, then store the additional fields. Optionally, override toString to combine the superclass message with domain fields. Remember to keep exception classes lightweight and focused: they should not hold heavy references or business logic. They are data carriers and signals. Finally, preserve the ability to chain a cause by providing a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause when wrapping lower-level exceptions. This combination of message, cause, and domain fields gives you the best debugging information while keeping handlers explicit about what they expect. InsufficientFundsException: class and fields means exception classes should provide message, cause, and domain getters to enable precise handling and diagnostics.. In practical terms, add domain data and useful constructors to a checked exception. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › InsufficientFundsException
Full example
// Custom Checked Exception with domain data
public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
  private double currentBalance;
  private double withdrawalAmount;

  public InsufficientFundsException(String message, double currentBalance, double withdrawalAmount) {
    super(message);
    this.currentBalance = currentBalance;
    this.withdrawalAmount = withdrawalAmount;
  }

  public InsufficientFundsException(String message, Throwable cause, double currentBalance, double withdrawalAmount) {
    super(message, cause);
    this.currentBalance = currentBalance;
    this.withdrawalAmount = withdrawalAmount;
  }

  public double getCurrentBalance() { return currentBalance; }
  public double getWithdrawalAmount() { return withdrawalAmount; }

  @Override
  public String toString() {
    return super.toString() + " [Balance: " + currentBalance + ", Attempted: " + withdrawalAmount + "]";
  }
}
Explanation
  • Provide constructors that match superclass patterns: message and message-plus-cause.
  • Store lightweight domain data with getters for handlers to use programmatically.
  • Avoid embedding business logic or heavy resources in exception objects.
  • Override toString only for richer logging; do not rely on it for programmatic behavior.
Check your understanding
Why add a constructor that accepts a cause? It preserves the original exception stack and message when wrapping lower-level errors.
Key Takeaway

Give exceptions structured data and cause-aware constructors so callers can react and debug effectively.

screens.title: BankAccount.withdraw and throws
screens.narratorSegment: The withdraw method demonstrates how a checked custom exception interacts with callers and the compiler. By declaring throws InsufficientFundsException in the method signature, withdraw communicates that it may fail due to business conditions beyond its control. Callers then must either catch the exception or also declare throws. Inside withdraw, perform input validation first, throw IllegalArgumentException for invalid input values, and then check business conditions such as insufficient balance. If the balance is insufficient, throw new InsufficientFundsException with the message and domain details. The practical effect is that the A P I contract now advertises this failure mode; it is part of the method's surface. This design helps higher layers decide how to present errors to users or perform compensating actions. Remember that throws only applies to checked exceptions: unchecked exceptions can still be thrown but are not required to be declared. Use method signatures to document expected recoverable failures and to push handling decisions up to the layer that has context to respond. In practical terms, declare throws to propagate checked exceptions to callers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › BankAccount.withdraw
BankAccount example
public class BankAccount {
  private String accountNumber;
  private double balance;

  public BankAccount(String accountNumber, double initialBalance) {
    this.accountNumber = accountNumber;
    this.balance = initialBalance;
  }

  public void deposit(double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Deposit amount must be positive.");
    this.balance += amount;
  }

  // Declares that it might throw the checked InsufficientFundsException
  public void withdraw(double amount) throws InsufficientFundsException {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Withdrawal amount must be positive.");
    if (this.balance < amount) {
      throw new InsufficientFundsException("Insufficient funds for withdrawal.", this.balance, amount);
    }
    this.balance -= amount;
  }

  public double getBalance() { return balance; }
}
Explanation & notes
  • The withdraw signature documents a recoverable business failure via throws.
  • Validate input using unchecked IllegalArgumentException for programming errors.
  • Throw the checked custom exception when the business rule fails so callers know to handle it.
  • Keep method contracts explicit: throws is both a compiler mechanism and runtime documentation.
Misconception
Declaring throws is not inefficient; it clarifies responsibilities and enables safer, documented error handling across layers.
Key Takeaway

Use throws to advertise recoverable failure modes and force higher-level code to make explicit decisions.

This allows precise messages or corrective actions. The catch block can also call printStackTrace or log getCause if the exception was wrapped. A common error is catching Exception broadly; prefer catching the specific custom type so you don't mistakenly hide other problems. That preserves the original stack trace and detailed root message, which is essential for debugging cross-layer failures. Always present concise, actionable information to users and detailed causes to logs. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Catching & Inspecting
BankApp main example
public class BankApp {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    BankAccount myAccount = new BankAccount("12345", 100.0);

    try {
      myAccount.deposit(50.0);
      myAccount.withdraw(200.0); // may throw InsufficientFundsException
      System.out.println("Withdrawal successful.");
    } catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {
      System.err.println("Transaction failed: " + e.getMessage());
      System.err.println("Current balance: " + e.getCurrentBalance());
      System.err.println("Attempted withdrawal: " + e.getWithdrawalAmount());
      if (e.getCause() != null) {
        System.err.println("Underlying cause: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
      }
      e.printStackTrace();
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
      System.err.println("Input error: " + e.getMessage());
    }

    System.out.println("Application finished.");
  }
}
Explanation
  • Caught InsufficientFundsException to provide specific feedback and corrective data to the user or caller.
  • Used getters to avoid parsing a message string, ensuring robust programmatic access to error details.
  • Checked getCause for wrapped exceptions when deeper diagnostics are needed.
  • Prefer narrow catches to avoid swallowing unrelated exceptions and masking bugs.
Common mistake

Catching Exception hides real problems; catch the domain-specific type to be explicit and safe.

screens.title: Exception Propagation and the throws Keyword
screens.narratorSegment: Exception propagation is the process by which an exception thrown in a method travels up through its callers until a matching catch block handles it or the program terminates. The throws keyword documents and enables propagation for checked exceptions by requiring either a catch or a throws declaration in each intermediate method. Conceptually, propagation is about responsibility: a lower-level component signals it cannot complete its work, and a higher-level component with more context decides whether to recover, compensate, or fail. In practice, you will choose which layer knows how to respond. For example, a repository method may declare throws DataAccessException, but a service layer may catch it and transform it into a business-level UserCreationException or retry the operation. A common misconception is that propagation is an exception to unit testing; in fact, testing should include scenarios where exceptions propagate and are properly translated or handled. Use throws intentionally to design clear contracts: it is both documentation for A P I users and a compile-time safety net for recoverable failure modes. Exception Propagation and the throws Keyword means use throws to escalate checked exceptions to layers that can make meaningful recovery or translation decisions.. In practical terms, how error responsibility moves up the call stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Propagation steps
Step 1
Throw a checked exception when a recoverable domain failure occurs.
Step 2
Intermediate methods either catch or declare throws to pass responsibility upward.
Step 3
A higher layer with context handles, retries, or wraps the error for its own API.
Example
A repository throws SQLException, the repository wraps it in a checked DataAccessException and declares throws. The service layer catches DataAccessException and throws a business-level UserCreationException to callers. This preserves details via getCause while exposing an API-appropriate error at the service boundary.
Misconception

Propagation is not a way to avoid handling; it is a design choice about which layer should know how to respond.

screens.title: Wrapping Exceptions Across Layers
screens.narratorSegment: Exception wrapping, or chaining, is the pattern of catching a low-level exception and throwing a new, higher-level exception that better expresses the current abstraction's failure mode, while passing the original exception as the cause. This preserves the original stack trace and root message via getCause, which is essential for debugging. In the UserRepository and UserService example, the repository encounters a SQLException, catches it, and throws new DataAccessException("Failed to save user", e). The service layer catches DataAccessException and rethrows a UserCreationException, again passing the DataAccessException as the cause. This creates a clear separation of concerns: the repository reports persistence faults, the service reports business-level user creation errors, and logging tools can inspect getCause to reveal the underlying SQLException. Avoid wrapping with overly generic messages that discard the original context. Also, avoid over-wrapping: multiple layers should only wrap when the abstraction changes and you want to present a different semantic error to callers. Preserving cause is not optional; include a cause constructor so debugging remains straightforward. Wrapping Exceptions Across Layers means wrap lower-level exceptions into domain-level exceptions and always pass the original exception as the cause for diagnostics.. In practical terms, translate low-level errors into business-level exceptions while preserving the cause. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Wrapping & Chaining
Repository example
public class DataAccessException extends Exception {
  public DataAccessException(String message, Throwable cause) {
    super(message, cause);
  }
}

public class UserRepository {
  public void saveUser(String username) throws DataAccessException {
    try {
      if (username.equals("admin")) {
        throw new java.sql.SQLException("Cannot save reserved username 'admin'.");
      }
      // persist user
    } catch (java.sql.SQLException e) {
      throw new DataAccessException("Failed to save user " + username + " to database.", e);
    }
  }
}
Service translation
public class UserCreationException extends Exception {
  public UserCreationException(String message, Throwable cause) {
    super(message, cause);
  }
}

public class UserService {
  private UserRepository repo = new UserRepository();

  public void createUser(String username, String password) {
    try {
      repo.saveUser(username);
    } catch (DataAccessException e) {
      throw new UserCreationException("Unable to create user", e);
    }
  }
}
Why preserve the cause?
getCause() returns the original exception, keeping its message and stack trace so logs and debuggers can reveal root-level failures while the API exposes a clearer, domain-oriented error.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Developers commonly make a few recurring mistakes when designing custom exceptions. First, creating too many tiny exception types for minor variations increases A P I surface and maintenance burden; prefer grouping when handling is identical. Second, catching overly broad types like Exception or Throwable hides unrelated failures and makes bugs harder to find. Third, throwing new exceptions without passing the original cause discards valuable debugging information; always use a cause-aware constructor when wrapping. Fourth, choosing unchecked when the caller can reasonably recover hides the obligation to handle expected conditions. Best practices to mitigate these mistakes include: document expected failure modes in method signatures with throws for checked exceptions, provide getters for structured error data rather than relying on message parsing, wrap lower-level exceptions with a clear higher-level message while passing the cause, and favor specific catches. Also consider evolution: if you expect callers to act differently on subclasses, design a small hierarchy; otherwise, use a single domain exception type with codes or fields. These guidelines keep error handling consistent, debuggable, and maintainable across a codebase. Common Mistakes and Best Practices means favor clarity: specific catches, cause preservation, and thoughtful exception granularity produce maintainable error handling.. In practical terms, avoid overuse, broad catches, and lost causes; prefer clarity and preserved context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In real applications, generic errors are not enough. You will learn why defining custom exceptions gives your code clearer contracts and richer diagnostics, and how exception propagation with the throws keyword moves responsibility up the call stack. We begin with the practical rationale: a banking withdrawal failure is more informative when represented by an InsufficientFundsException than by a generic illegal argument or runtime error. That clarity makes handling behavior explicit for callers and enables richer logging and automated responses. We'll also show the mechanical differences between checked and unchecked exceptions, when the compiler enforces handling, and when it doesn't. Finally, we'll explore exception wrapping, where lower-level causes are preserved as the underlying reason for a higher-level, domain-focused exception. As we progress, you will see code patterns for creating exceptions, declaring throws, catching and rethrowing with a cause, and trade-offs to avoid over-creating tiny exception types. By the end of this lesson, you will understand how to represent domain rules with types, propagate errors cleanly, and wrap exceptions so that the original stack and message remain available for debugging. Consider an error you recently handled: would a custom exception have made handling clearer?

By the end of this chapter you will design and implement custom checked and unchecked exceptions, choose the appropriate exception type for a domain error, and use constructors to carry error details. You will understand exception propagation: how the throws keyword delegates responsibility to a caller and how an exception travels up the call stack until handled. You will practice rethrowing and wrapping exceptions so that higher-level layers see business-friendly error types while lower-level causes remain accessible through getCause. You will also learn practical restraints: avoid excessive tiny exception classes, prefer checked exceptions for recoverable, anticipated problems, and reserve unchecked exceptions for programming or unrecoverable errors. Each objective is mapped to a verified competency milestone that shows you how to test and confirm mastery: create a checked InsufficientFundsException with getters and handle it in calling code; implement a DataAccessException that wraps a SQLException and use getCause to log root failures. These skills make error handling explicit, maintainable, and easier to debug in layered applications.

This chapter pairs explanation with concrete coding tasks. You'll create a checked InsufficientFundsException and an unchecked InvalidAccountIdFormatException, then use them inside a BankAccount class to observe compiler behavior. Later you'll implement a DataAccessException that wraps S Q L errors, and write a UserService that rethrows the wrapped exception for business-level handling. The practical inventory activity guides you to create InvalidProductDataException and ProductInitializationError and validate name and stock rules in a Product constructor. Each exercise reinforces a trade-off: checked exceptions make callers aware of recoverable conditions, unchecked exceptions represent programmer or unrecoverable errors. We'll also examine common mistakes like over-abundant tiny exceptions and catching overly broad exception types which hide real bugs. For assessment, you'll reason about a createUser pattern that correctly wraps a DatabaseConnectionException into a UserCreationException. These tasks build muscle memory for declaring throws, using constructors that accept a cause, calling getCause for diagnostics, and deciding at what layer to handle or propagate an error.

A custom exception is simply a user-defined class that extends an existing throwable type in Java. When you extend Exception you create a checked exception: the compiler forces callers to handle or declare it. When you extend RuntimeException you create an unchecked exception: callers are not forced by the compiler to catch or declare it. The key value of a custom exception is representation. Instead of treating every failure as a generic illegal argument or null pointer, a meaningful type like InsufficientFundsException signals the exact business rule that failed and can carry structured data such as a current balance and attempted withdrawal amount. This lets handlers react differently depending on the failure type, and allows logging or automated responses that reference domain details. A common misconception is that more exception classes mean better code. In practice you should create a custom exception when its type communicates intent or enables specific handling. If the standard java exceptions already express the condition and no extra behavior or data is required, prefer the built-in types. Think of custom exceptions as part of your A P I contract: they make legal, recoverable failure modes explicit and discoverable to callers.

Checked exceptions extend Exception and require callers to either catch them or declare them with throws. They are appropriate for anticipated, recoverable external conditions such as validation failures, input and output problems, or business rules the caller can reasonably address. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are not enforced by the compiler. Use them for programming errors or unrecoverable conditions where forcing callers to catch them would add noise. A common example in the chapter is InvalidAccountIdFormatException as an unchecked exception: an invalid format often indicates a programming or input validation bug that should be fixed rather than caught repeatedly. A mistake learners make is choosing unchecked for recoverable conditions, which hides the obligation to handle an expected failure. Conversely, overusing checked exceptions can force many try-catch blocks that clutter control flow. Think in terms of responsibility: if a caller can reasonably recover or present corrective UI, prefer a checked exception. If the failure signals a bug or unrecoverable state, prefer unchecked. For clarity, include constructors for message and cause, and attach domain fields when callers need them. This comparison helps you design the right contract for library and application layers.

Here we walk through a typical checked custom exception that carries domain information. The InsufficientFundsException extends Exception, includes fields for the current balance and attempted withdrawal, and provides constructors that accept a message and these values. Why include fields? Because handlers often need those numeric details to log, show a corrective message, or compute alternative flows. A common pitfall is only passing a message string; structured getters are more reliable for automated handling. Notice the implementation pattern: call super(message) to initialize the base Throwable message, then store the additional fields. Optionally, override toString to combine the superclass message with domain fields. Remember to keep exception classes lightweight and focused: they should not hold heavy references or business logic. They are data carriers and signals. Finally, preserve the ability to chain a cause by providing a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause when wrapping lower-level exceptions. This combination of message, cause, and domain fields gives you the best debugging information while keeping handlers explicit about what they expect. InsufficientFundsException: class and fields means exception classes should provide message, cause, and domain getters to enable precise handling and diagnostics.. In practical terms, add domain data and useful constructors to a checked exception. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The withdraw method demonstrates how a checked custom exception interacts with callers and the compiler. By declaring throws InsufficientFundsException in the method signature, withdraw communicates that it may fail due to business conditions beyond its control. Callers then must either catch the exception or also declare throws. Inside withdraw, perform input validation first, throw IllegalArgumentException for invalid input values, and then check business conditions such as insufficient balance. If the balance is insufficient, throw new InsufficientFundsException with the message and domain details. The practical effect is that the A P I contract now advertises this failure mode; it is part of the method's surface. This design helps higher layers decide how to present errors to users or perform compensating actions. Remember that throws only applies to checked exceptions: unchecked exceptions can still be thrown but are not required to be declared. Use method signatures to document expected recoverable failures and to push handling decisions up to the layer that has context to respond. In practical terms, declare throws to propagate checked exceptions to callers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a caller receives a checked custom exception, it can extract the domain data or present a user-friendly message. In the BankApp example, main calls deposit and withdraw inside a try block and catches InsufficientFundsException to provide specific feedback: the exception's getters reveal the current balance and attempted withdrawal. This allows precise messages or corrective actions. The catch block can also call printStackTrace or log getCause if the exception was wrapped. A common error is catching Exception broadly; prefer catching the specific custom type so you don't mistakenly hide other problems. If a method can do more useful recovery in a higher layer, handle it there; otherwise declare throws and let a higher-level component manage the response. When logging, include both the custom message and any cause: e. getCause() returns the wrapped lower-level error when exception chaining was used. That preserves the original stack trace and detailed root message, which is essential for debugging cross-layer failures. Always present concise, actionable information to users and detailed causes to logs. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Exception propagation is the process by which an exception thrown in a method travels up through its callers until a matching catch block handles it or the program terminates. The throws keyword documents and enables propagation for checked exceptions by requiring either a catch or a throws declaration in each intermediate method. Conceptually, propagation is about responsibility: a lower-level component signals it cannot complete its work, and a higher-level component with more context decides whether to recover, compensate, or fail. In practice, you will choose which layer knows how to respond. For example, a repository method may declare throws DataAccessException, but a service layer may catch it and transform it into a business-level UserCreationException or retry the operation. A common misconception is that propagation is an exception to unit testing; in fact, testing should include scenarios where exceptions propagate and are properly translated or handled. Use throws intentionally to design clear contracts: it is both documentation for A P I users and a compile-time safety net for recoverable failure modes. Exception wrapping, or chaining, is the pattern of catching a low-level exception and throwing a new, higher-level exception that better expresses the current abstraction's failure mode, while passing the original exception as the cause. This preserves the original stack trace and root message via getCause, which is essential for debugging. In the UserRepository and UserService example, the repository encounters a SQLException, catches it, and throws new DataAccessException("Failed to save user", e). The service layer catches DataAccessException and rethrows a UserCreationException, again passing the DataAccessException as the cause. This creates a clear separation of concerns: the repository reports persistence faults, the service reports business-level user creation errors, and logging tools can inspect getCause to reveal the underlying SQLException. Avoid wrapping with overly generic messages that discard the original context. Also, avoid over-wrapping: multiple layers should only wrap when the abstraction changes and you want to present a different semantic error to callers. Preserving cause is not optional; include a cause constructor so debugging remains straightforward. Developers commonly make a few recurring mistakes when designing custom exceptions. First, creating too many tiny exception types for minor variations increases A P I surface and maintenance burden; prefer grouping when handling is identical. Second, catching overly broad types like Exception or Throwable hides unrelated failures and makes bugs harder to find. Third, throwing new exceptions without passing the original cause discards valuable debugging information; always use a cause-aware constructor when wrapping. Fourth, choosing unchecked when the caller can reasonably recover hides the obligation to handle expected conditions. Best practices to mitigate these mistakes include: document expected failure modes in method signatures with throws for checked exceptions, provide getters for structured error data rather than relying on message parsing, wrap lower-level exceptions with a clear higher-level message while passing the cause, and favor specific catches. Also consider evolution: if you expect callers to act differently on subclasses, design a small hierarchy; otherwise, use a single domain exception type with codes or fields. These guidelines keep error handling consistent, debuggable, and maintainable across a codebase. To summarize, custom exceptions let you express domain failures as types with optional structured data so handlers can react precisely. Choose checked exceptions when callers should be forced to handle a recoverable condition, and unchecked exceptions for programming errors or unrecoverable initialization faults. Use throws to declare checked exceptions and propagate responsibility up the stack, and wrap lower-level exceptions with higher-level ones to preserve abstraction while keeping the original cause accessible via getCause. Avoid over-granularity in exception types, catching overly broad exceptions, and dropping the cause when wrapping. These practices lead to clearer APIs, more maintainable error handling, and better diagnostics when failures occur.
